metadata.methods_description: Participants watched instructional videos in two attention conditions: attentive viewing, followed by memory questions, and distracted viewing, in which they silently counted backwards from a random prime number in steps of 7. EEG, EOG, ECG, respiration, pupillary responses, gaze, and head position were recorded. Questionnaires included domain-knowledge and memory questions and the ASRS adult ADHD symptom checklist.

citation_details.title: Attentional state, not trait, predicts test performance in video-based learning
citation_details.author: Jens Madsen, Lucas C. Parra
citation_details.abstract: Summary Poor academic performance is often linked to attention deficits, but it remains unclear whether these reflect enduring traits or momentary lapses in focus. In this study, we examined how state and trait-level attention relate to learning from short educational videos. Across four experiments (N = 152), participants completed standardized assessments of inattention, hyperactivity, working memory capacity, and GPA. They then viewed 3-6-minute educational videos while electroencephalography (EEG) tracked neural responses, followed by quizzes assessing short-term retention. Neural synchrony during video viewing, a measure of attentional state, strongly predicted test performance (p < 0.001). In contrast, trait inattention did not predict retention (p > 0.05), although it was negatively associated with GPA. citation_details.venue: 2026 IEEE International Research Conference on Smart Computing and Systems Engineering (SCSE)
citation_details.abstract: In recent years, video-based learning has emerged as a prominent instructional approach for enhancing learner engagement in digital education. However, sustaining attention in such multimedia environments remains a critical challenge, particularly in the absence of real-time cognitive feedback. Electroencephalography (EEG) has gained increasing attention as a non-invasive neurophysiological tool for objectively assessing attentional states through brainwave patterns associated with cognitive processing. This systematic literature review examines EEG-based attention assessment techniques in video-based learning environments, grounded in Schema Theory, a cognitive framework that emphasizes the role of prior knowledge structures in guiding attention and learning. citation_details.author: Tasikala Rathnayake, Subodha Subasingha, Malithi Nawarathne, Prasanna Sumathipala, Anjana Junius Vidanaralage
citation_details.venue: 2026 IEEE International Research Conference on Smart Computing and Systems Engineering (SCSE)
citation_details.abstract: Monitoring learner attention during video-based learning is important for adaptive educational systems. However, common indicators such as clicks, video completion, and quiz scores do not directly reflect whether learners remain attentive. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a noninvasive and time-sensitive measure of brain activity for attention-state assessment. This study investigates whether interpretable EEG spectral features can classify attentive and distracted states during instructional video viewing. EEG recordings from 30 participants in Experiment 2 of the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset (BBBD) were analyzed using the common stimulus stim01 under attentive and distracted conditions. The signals were segmented into 4 s windows with 2 s overlap, producing 5278 windows (2730 attentive, 2548 distracted). citation_details.author: Zi-Kang Leng, Edan Eyal, Ying-Tian Shi, Jia-Man He, Ya-Qi Liu, T. Plötz
citation_details.abstract: Engagement, which links to attentional, emotional, and cognitive dimensions, plays an important role in learning. In online and video-based learning environments, learners often need to regulate their own interactions with instructional materials. Measuring and reflecting on engagement can therefore support both learners and adaptive learning systems. In this study, we use wearable and camera-based sensing devices to collect physiological and motion signals, including PPG, ECG, EDA, EEG, IMU, heart rate, temperature, and eye-tracking data, to estimate learner engagement.
